planting.note: Grow in very well-drained, mineral, gritty succulent mix with added limestone chips or coarse sand in bright light; Titanopsis needs excellent drainage and a lean, low-organic soil to avoid rot.

directions: Grow in very well-drained, mineral, gritty succulent mix in bright light to full sun. Titanopsis calcarea forms low, spreading clusters of thick, triangular, blue-grey leaves with warty, crystalline-textured tips that closely mimic the rough limestone rock formations of its native South African habitat, an unusual camouflage texture distinct from the smooth, stone-mimicking bodies of Lithops and Pleiospilos. Bright yellow to orange daisy-like flowers appear from among the leaf clusters in fall to winter. It tolerates slightly more routine watering than true Lithops but still needs sharp drainage and a lean, low-organic mix, since rich or constantly moist soil quickly leads to rot in the crystalline-tipped leaves. Provide the brightest light available for the most compact growth and best texture development.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow in very well-drained, mineral, gritty succulent mix in bright light to full sun; Faucaria tuberculosa needs a fall to winter rest with reduced water.

directions: Grow in very well-drained, mineral, gritty succulent mix in bright light to full sun. Faucaria tuberculosa is a close relative of the better-known Tiger Jaws, sharing the same opposite pairs of triangular, spine-toothed leaves that resemble an open jaw, but with a distinctly warty, raised, pebbled leaf surface texture that sets it apart from the smoother-leaved species. Large, bright yellow, daisy-like flowers open in late afternoon to evening in fall, closing again by the following midday. It forms a dense, clumping rosette that spreads slowly by offsets, and blooms most reliably when given strong light and a period of cooler, drier conditions in fall. Water moderately during the growing season, allowing the mix to dry between waterings, and reduce water further in winter to prevent rot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow in very well-drained, mineral, gritty succulent mix in bright light; Argyroderma follows a strict seasonal cycle similar to Lithops, needing minimal water while the old leaf pair is being reabsorbed and a dry summer rest.

directions: Grow in very well-drained, mineral, gritty succulent mix in bright light to full sun, following the plant's strict seasonal watering cycle. Argyroderma delaetii, commonly called living granite, forms small, rounded, fused leaf pairs in shades of grey-green to silvery-white that closely resemble smooth granite pebbles, one of the most convincing stone-mimicry succulents alongside its relatives Lithops and Conophytum. Large, showy, magenta-pink to purple or occasionally yellow daisy-like flowers, often nearly as wide as the plant body, appear in late summer to fall. As with Lithops, each new leaf pair draws moisture from and eventually replaces the old pair, which shrivels and is shed, so watering must be withheld during this transition and through the plant's dry summer dormancy to avoid splitting or rot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow in very well-drained, mineral, gritty succulent mix in bright light to full sun; the swollen caudex (base) develops best when the plant is grown in a shallow pot that exposes part of the root to light and air.

directions: Grow in very well-drained, mineral, gritty succulent mix in bright light to full sun. Trichodiadema bulbosum develops a swollen, woody, bulbous caudex (thickened base) over time, topped with slender branches bearing small, cylindrical green leaves each tipped with a crown of fine, star-like white bristles, giving the growing tips a bristly, diadem-like appearance that gives the genus its name. As the caudex thickens with age, growers often raise it partially above the soil surface to display it, giving the plant a gnarled, tree-like, bonsai appearance in miniature. Small pink to magenta daisy-like flowers appear on the branch tips in the growing season. Water moderately when actively growing, allowing the mix to dry between waterings, and reduce water in winter to protect the caudex from rot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
